svg.aria-label: Diagram: what the Amazon Bedrock product attributes billing dimension adds to AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets and AWS Cost Management Dashboards, and the consequence of the asymmetry between those tools. AWS states that Cost Explorer, Budgets and Cost Management Dashboards now let you analyze Amazon Bedrock costs by product attributes, a new dimension that breaks down Bedrock cost by model, model provider, inference type and feature. The four attributes are listed with AWS's own examples: model, such as Claude Sonnet 5 or Claude Haiku 4.5; model provider, such as Anthropic or Cohere; inference type, such as input tokens or output tokens; and feature, such as on-demand inference or reranker. Of those four, inference type is the one that points at a change the reader can make, because it separates input token spend from output token spend and those are driven by different things, prompt and context size on one side and generation length on the other, whereas the model attribute identifies which model is expensive rather than why. The central asymmetry is in the verbs AWS uses: in Cost Explorer and Dashboards you can group and filter costs by these attributes, but in Budgets you can only filter budgets by the same attributes. Grouping produces one view broken out by every value of the attribute, so a single Cost Explorer view or dashboard widget covers every model including models adopted after the view was built, and it needs no maintenance. Filtering selects a subset, so a budget scoped to one model covers that model alone, and AWS's own example confirms the singular by describing setting a budget that alerts on spend for a single model. The operational consequence is that per-model budget alerting requires one budget per model, that the set of budgets has to be maintained as model choice changes, and that a model adopted by a team after the budgets were created falls outside every per-model budget while still counting toward any total Bedrock budget, so the gap is in the per-model alerting layer rather than in the overall ceiling, and the budgets keep passing because the thing they watch has not changed. The recommended shape is therefore a total Bedrock budget that cannot develop a gap, plus per-model budgets for the models that matter most, plus a grouped Cost Explorer view or dashboard widget as the thing that actually reveals a newly adopted model. Attribution comes from combining the dimension with tags: cost allocation tags on application inference profiles, projects or workspaces answer which applications drive spend on each model, and IAM principal tags answer which users or roles drive it, which also means project and workspace names travel into finance reports and the remedy is a naming convention rather than a permission. A note of caution records that the announcement does not state whether the new dimension applies to historical spend predating the launch, and that cost allocation tags and AWS-supplied dimensions have historically behaved differently in that respect, so retroactive coverage is something to check in the console rather than assume. On availability and cost, AWS states the dimension is available today at no additional charge in all AWS Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud US Regions and the China Beijing and China Ningxia Regions.
svg.title: Group gives you every model in one view; filter gives you one model per budget
svg.text: The whole post is the difference between two verbs.
Amazon Bedrock product attributes — a new billing dimension in Cost Explorer, Budgets and Dashboards.
Four attributes, with AWS’s own examples
model — “Claude Sonnet 5 or Claude Haiku 4.5” model provider — “Anthropic or Cohere”
inference type — “input tokens or output tokens” feature — “on-demand inference or reranker”
inference type is the only one that points at a change you can make.
model says which is expensive; input-vs-output says why — context size on one side, generation length on the other.
GROUP — Cost Explorer & Dashboards
“you can group and filter costs by these attributes”
One view, broken out by every value.
Covers models adopted after you built it.
Maintenance: none
Reporting, though — somebody still has to look at it.
FILTER — Budgets, and only filter
“In Budgets, you can filter budgets by the same
attributes”
Selects a subset → one budget per model.
AWS’s own example keeps the singular: “a budget that
alerts on spend for a single model”
Maintenance: a list, revisited when models change
vs
The gap that widens quietly
A model a team adopts next week is inside your total Bedrock budget and outside every per-model one.
And the budgets keep passing — the thing they watch has not changed.
So build three things, not one
1 · A total Bedrock budget, unfiltered — the only one that cannot develop a gap. No maintenance.
2 · Per-model budgets for the models that matter — with the review date written down somewhere.
3 · A grouped view or dashboard widget — the control that actually surfaces a new model.
Group for coverage, filter for alerting, and know which one you built.
Attribution comes from combining
tags on “application inference profiles, projects, or
workspaces” → which applications drive spend
“IAM principal tags” → which users or roles do
Two things to check, not assume
Retroactivity. The announcement is silent on spend
before launch. Tags are not retroactive; dimensions
usually differ. Check the console, do not promise it.
Project names travel into finance reports — that is a naming convention, not a permission.
“available today at no additional charge in all AWS Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China (Beijing)
and China (Ningxia) Regions” — so the dimension is free, and three Regions do not have it.
